working-capital|restaurants-and-hospital.h1: Working capital finance for restaurants and hospitality
working-capital|restaurants-and-hospital.title: Working Capital for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
working-capital|restaurants-and-hospital.desc: How UK restaurants, cafés, pubs and hotels cover the gap between daily costs and quiet months, and which finance types usually suit. Free introduction.
working-capital|restaurants-and-hospital.lead: Takings arrive daily, but rent, wages and VAT arrive in lumps, and January is long.
intro: A restaurant or pub is paid almost immediately, by card on the night, yet most of its costs are settled weeks later or in a single hit. Suppliers want paying on 14 or 30 days, rent falls due quarterly, and a VAT bill can land just after a thin month. Working capital in hospitality is rarely about waiting for customers to pay. It is about smoothing the shape of the year, so that a strong December does not have to carry a weak February.

Because lenders can see card takings in the bank statements, the finance that tends to suit is the kind that follows them. A merchant cash advance is repaid as a share of card sales, a revolving credit facility gives a limit to draw on and repay, and a short-term unsecured loan can cover a one-off squeeze. Invoice finance usually only fits venues that bill corporate clients, such as a hotel with function and events business.
uses: Getting through January and February
Cover wages, rent and supplier bills for the eight or so weeks when covers drop, then repay as spring and summer trade returns.
Stocking up before a peak
Buy extra food, drink and linen ahead of Christmas or a bank holiday weekend, when suppliers want paying before the extra takings come in.
A quarterly VAT or rent bill
Spread a large quarter-end payment across a few months so it does not land on the same week as payroll.
Hotels waiting on corporate accounts
Bridge the 30 to 60 days between hosting a conference or wedding party and the invoice being paid.
fit: Repayments that follow trade

A merchant cash advance is repaid from a percentage of daily card sales, so a quiet week costs less than a busy one. It suits venues with steady card volume, and it is usually quicker to arrange than a bank loan. The total repaid is higher than the amount advanced, so a broker will show you the full cost before you decide.
A limit to dip into

A revolving credit facility works like a business overdraft with a set limit: draw in the lean weeks, repay when takings recover, and pay interest only on what is used. Lenders usually look at 12 months of statements to see how takings move through the seasons, and some ask for a director’s guarantee.
Small, short-term borrowing

For a one-off squeeze, an unsecured loan of, for example, £15,000 to £50,000 over 6 to 24 months is common. No asset is pledged, but lenders will look at card turnover, the age of the business and how consistently the account stays in credit.
considerations: Seasonal repayments are not free
A fixed monthly repayment feels heavy in a quiet month. If trade is strongly seasonal, ask a broker whether a flexible or card-linked repayment suits better than a fixed schedule.
Borrowing to cover losses
If the venue is losing money in a normal month, extra working capital delays the problem rather than fixing it. Lenders will look at margins, so it is worth checking food and labour costs first.
Rent and lease length
A short lease with little time left can limit what lenders will offer. A broker may suggest asset finance for specific equipment instead of general borrowing.
faqs: Do restaurants need security to borrow for working capital?

Not always. Merchant cash advances and many unsecured loans do not need a charge over property or equipment. Some lenders ask for a personal guarantee from a director, which means you could be liable if the company cannot repay. A broker can explain which products ask for one before you apply.
Which finance follows card takings most closely?

A merchant cash advance is repaid as a fixed share of card sales, so repayments rise and fall with trade. It only suits venues that take a good volume of card payments through a single provider. The total repayable is set in advance, and a broker should show you the cost clearly.
How much working capital might a café or pub borrow?

It depends on turnover and costs. As an illustration, a pub with £600,000 annual takings might look at a facility of £20,000 to £60,000 to cover quiet months. Lenders decide on the business’s trading history and bank statements, so amounts vary widely from one venue to the next.
Can a business with a new venue still borrow?

The company usually needs to have been trading for at least six months, and lenders often look for 12 months of statements to see a full seasonal pattern. A second venue that has just opened may be assessed alongside the first, so the group’s combined accounts can matter.
Is it better to borrow for quiet months or build reserves?

Reserves cost nothing, but building them takes a few strong years and one big repair can wipe them out. Many venues use a flexible facility as a back-up. A broker can explain the costs and let you weigh them against the cash you would otherwise tie up.

business-expansion|restaurants-and-hospi.h1: Business expansion finance for restaurants and hospitality
business-expansion|restaurants-and-hospi.title: Business Expansion Finance for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
business-expansion|restaurants-and-hospi.desc: How UK restaurants, pubs, cafés and hotels finance a second site, a refit or a bigger kitchen, and which finance types tend to suit. Free introduction.
business-expansion|restaurants-and-hospi.lead: A second site or a bigger kitchen costs money months before the first full week of takings.
intro: Expanding a venue means paying for the fit-out, the deposit, the pre-opening staff and the first stock before a single cover is sold. A new restaurant might take three to six months to find its feet, and many lenders know that. They tend to look hard at how the first site performs, because a strong original is the best evidence that a second can work. The size of the ask also matters: opening another site is a very different request from adding a terrace.

Different parts of an expansion tend to suit different finance. Kitchen and bar equipment can be financed on its own, with the kit as security. A fit-out or lease premium often needs a term loan, secured or unsecured. Buying the freehold of a site may fit a commercial mortgage. A broker who knows hospitality can split the project so each piece is financed in the way that costs least and strains cash flow least.
uses: Opening a second restaurant
Cover the lease deposit, fit-out, opening stock and a few months of staff costs while the new site builds up trade.
Adding a terrace or extra covers
Pay for building work, outdoor heating and furniture to add seats that earn their keep through the warmer months.
A new kitchen or bar
Install a larger kitchen, a cocktail bar or a bakery counter to widen the menu and raise average spend.
Buying the building
Move from renting to owning a site, so rent becomes a mortgage payment and the business holds an asset.
fit: Equipment financed separately

Ovens, extraction, chillers and coffee machines can be financed through asset finance, often over three to five years, with the equipment as security. This keeps the larger fit-out budget free for the parts nothing can be repossessed from, such as design and labour.
A term loan for the fit-out

A fit-out loan of, for example, £80,000 to £250,000 over three to seven years is common for a second site. Lenders usually ask for the first venue’s accounts, a business plan with projected covers and spend, and the signed lease or heads of terms for the new premises.
Property and longer terms

If the business is buying the site, a commercial mortgage can run for 10 to 25 years, usually with a deposit of 25% or more. Lenders will look at the valuation, the trading history at that address, and whether the company’s profits cover the repayments comfortably.
considerations: Ramp-up costs are easy to underestimate
New venues tend to lose money in the first months. A broker may suggest including a working capital buffer in the borrowing, so the first quiet fortnight does not threaten the repayments.
Personal guarantees
Many expansion loans for hospitality venues ask for a director’s guarantee. Read what it commits you to before signing, since your personal assets may be at risk if the company cannot repay.
When expansion is not the answer
If the original site is not yet reliably profitable, adding a second can stretch both. A refit of the first site may deliver more at lower risk.
faqs: Can I finance a second restaurant before it opens?

Yes, lenders do consider this, but they look mainly at the first venue’s trading history and your plans for the second. The business must be trading for at least six months and usually needs 12 months of accounts. A signed lease or heads of terms strengthens the case.
What do lenders want to see for a hospitality expansion?

Typically bank statements, recent accounts, a business plan with projected sales and costs, and details of the new premises. They look at how the existing venue performs through the year and whether its profits could service the new borrowing even if the new site takes time to build trade.
Should equipment be financed separately from the fit-out?

Often, yes. Equipment is easy for a lender to value and take as security, so it can attract simpler terms. Keeping it separate leaves the term loan for building and design costs. A broker can lay out both routes so you can compare monthly costs together.
Is a commercial mortgage realistic for a restaurant owner?

It can be, if the company has a solid trading record and a deposit. Lenders will check the lease or title, the valuation and trading performance at the address. Some will lend on pubs and hotels as trading businesses, which is a specialist area that suits a broker with that experience.
What if the new site is slower to build than planned?

This is a real risk. Repayments are due whether or not covers match the forecast, so many brokers suggest borrowing slightly more for a buffer, or choosing a longer term to lower monthly payments. A broker will also explain how much headroom lenders expect in your forecasts.

working-capital|construction-and-trades.h1: Working capital finance for construction and trades
working-capital|construction-and-trades.title: Working Capital for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
working-capital|construction-and-trades.desc: How UK builders, electricians, plumbers and contractors cover materials, wages and slow payments, and which finance types tend to suit. Free introduction.
working-capital|construction-and-trades.lead: Materials and wages go out on day one, while stage payments and retentions come in months later.
intro: Contractors pay for labour and materials as a job runs, then wait for valuations to be certified, invoices to be approved and payments to clear. On commercial work, 45 to 60 days is normal, and the main contractor will often hold back 3% to 5% as retention until the defects period ends, which can be a year or more after the job finishes. A busy, profitable firm can still run short of cash because its money is sitting on other people’s balance sheets.

This makes invoice finance one of the more natural fits, since the money owed is already documented on invoices and valuations. A revolving credit facility can smooth wages and merchant accounts, and a short-term unsecured loan can cover a gap before a big payment lands. Trade counter accounts, VAT and CIS deductions add their own timing wrinkles, so a broker used to construction can help match the facility to the way you are actually paid.
uses: Waiting on a stage payment
Pay wages and subcontractors while a valuation is certified and an invoice moves through the client’s approval process.
Buying materials for a big job
Pay a merchant for steel, timber, cable or plant hire up front, on a job that will only pay out in stages.
Releasing the retention gap
Release part of the 3% to 5% held back on completed jobs, so it does not sit unpaid for a year.
Paying subcontractors on time
Meet weekly or fortnightly labour costs on days when the client’s payment is still weeks away.
fit: Invoice finance on certified work

Lenders advance a large share of the value of approved invoices, often 80% to 90%, and release the rest less fees when the client pays. It works best when the customers are other businesses, councils or main contractors, with a clear invoice trail. Lenders check the customer’s credit standing as well as yours.
Retentions and staged work

Retentions can be harder to finance than normal invoices because they are payable on a future condition. Some invoice finance providers will advance against them, usually at a lower percentage, while others exclude them. A broker can say which providers are open to it.
A revolving facility for the weekly cycle

A revolving credit facility of, for example, £30,000 to £150,000 can fund weekly wages and supplier accounts, then be repaid as stage payments arrive. Lenders look at turnover, margins and how reliably the account moves back into credit.
considerations: Disputes and variations
Invoice finance depends on invoices being accepted. If a client disputes a variation or a defect, the advance may be reclaimed. Keep valuations signed off and records tidy.
Confidentiality
Some invoice finance arrangements are disclosed, meaning customers pay the lender directly. Others are confidential. Ask your broker which suits the relationship with your main contractor.
Chronic slow payment
If every client pays 90 days late, borrowing only papers over a pricing or terms problem. A broker may suggest tightening credit terms or asking for deposits on larger orders.
faqs: Can I get invoice finance on a construction invoice?

Often yes, if the invoice is for completed, certified work owed by another business. Lenders are cautious about invoices for work in progress or subject to retention, because the payment depends on future conditions. A broker who knows construction can point to providers who accept these.
Do CIS deductions affect working capital borrowing?

Indirectly. If you are a subcontractor paid net of CIS deductions, your cash received is lower than the invoice value for a time. Lenders will see the pattern in your statements, and invoice finance is usually calculated on the gross invoice, so a broker can explain how deductions are handled.
How much working capital might a small firm borrow?

As an illustration, a firm turning over £800,000 might look at a facility of £40,000 to £120,000. Actual limits depend on turnover, margins, the age of the business and, for invoice finance, the quality of the invoices. A broker can give a clearer sense after hearing the details.
Is a personal guarantee likely?

Often for smaller firms, yes. Invoice finance, revolving credit and loans can all ask for a director’s guarantee, and some also take a debenture over company assets. A broker will explain what each lender requires before you commit to a facility.
What if I only need cover for a single large job?

A short-term unsecured loan or a facility tied to that contract may be enough. Lenders will ask about the contract value, the payment schedule and the client. If the client is a large, creditworthy company, it often helps, and a broker can match the borrowing to the job.

business-expansion|construction-and-trad.h1: Business expansion finance for construction and trades
business-expansion|construction-and-trad.title: Business Expansion Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
business-expansion|construction-and-trad.desc: How UK contractors and trades businesses finance bigger contracts, new vans and plant, and a new depot, and which finance tends to suit. Free introduction.
business-expansion|construction-and-trad.lead: Bigger contracts need more plant, vans and people up front, before the first payment arrives.
intro: Growing a trades business usually means winning work that is bigger than the firm’s current kit and cash. A contractor moving from domestic jobs to commercial fit-outs needs more operatives, higher insurance limits, extra vans and often a depot. All of it is paid for ahead of the first stage payment, and larger clients often come with longer payment terms and retentions, which stretch the gap further. That is the central problem a growing trades firm has to plan for.

Expansion in construction is therefore usually financed in layers. Vehicles and plant suit asset finance, because each item is easy to value and the loan is secured on it. A depot or yard may suit a commercial mortgage. The extra working capital needed to carry a larger contract is often best handled with invoice finance or a revolving facility, rather than a bigger fixed loan. A broker can help build those layers into a single plan.
uses: Moving into commercial work
Take on larger tenders by paying for the extra staff, insurance and equipment before the first valuation is paid.
Adding vans and plant
Buy or lease vehicles, a digger, access platforms or scaffolding so more crews can work at once.
A depot or yard
Move from a garage or home base to premises with storage, parking and an office as the team grows.
A second trade or region
Open a branch in a new area, or add a related trade such as groundworks or roofing, and cover the cost of the first hires.
fit: Vehicles and plant through asset finance

Asset finance usually covers most or all of the price of a van, excavator or access platform, with repayments over two to five years and the asset as security. Plant holds its value well, particularly with recognised makes, and lenders look at the age of the asset and your trading record.
A depot through a commercial mortgage

A yard or workshop bought through a commercial mortgage might run for 10 to 25 years with a deposit of around 25%. Lenders will look at the property’s value and use, planning and environmental issues for yards, and whether profits cover the repayments with room to spare.
Working capital for the larger contract

Bigger contracts bring bigger gaps. For example, a £400,000 contract on 60-day terms may need £100,000 or more in labour and materials before the first payment. Invoice finance or a revolving facility can scale with the work, where a fixed loan would be sized once and could be too small.
considerations: Growth can outrun cash
Taking on more work than your cash can carry is a common reason for contractors to struggle. Build the working capital for the new work into the plan, not just the equipment.
Idle kit is expensive
Plant and vans are repaid whether or not they are working. Check there is enough work booked to keep new equipment busy before taking it on.
Tender requirements
Some larger clients ask for evidence of financial standing or particular insurance levels. A broker may suggest putting finance in place before you tender.
faqs: Can a small contractor finance plant and vehicles?

Yes, asset finance is widely used for this. The equipment itself is the security, so lenders may be more flexible than with unsecured borrowing. They will still look at the company’s trading history, accounts and the type and age of the asset, and some ask for a deposit.
What is the difference between hire purchase and leasing for a van?

With hire purchase you usually own the van at the end after the final payment, and with leasing you generally return it or pay to keep it. VAT and tax treatment differ, so a broker or accountant can explain which suits the way your business is set up.
Will lenders finance a depot for a trades business?

A commercial mortgage can be used, but lenders will consider the type of property, the planning use and the company’s profits. Light industrial units are commonly financed. The business typically needs to have been trading for a while and have a deposit ready.
How much extra working capital does a bigger contract need?

It depends on payment terms and the mix of labour and materials. As an illustration, if you pay £60,000 a month in costs and are paid 60 days after valuation, you may need £120,000 or more outstanding at the peak. A broker can help estimate this before you commit to a tender.
Is expanding into a new region too risky?

It carries more risk than growing where you are known, because local reputation and relationships take time to build. Lenders will want to see the existing business is stable and profitable. A staged approach, such as one extra crew first, is easier to finance than a full branch.

working-capital|retail.h1: Working capital finance for retail businesses
working-capital|retail.title: Working Capital for Retail Businesses | Loanleaf
working-capital|retail.desc: How UK shops and retailers pay suppliers for stock months before it sells, and which finance types tend to suit a retail cash cycle. Free introduction.
working-capital|retail.lead: A retailer pays for stock first and is paid only when it sells, which can be months later.
intro: Retail cash flow runs backwards. Stock is ordered, often in bulk and sometimes from overseas, then paid for before it reaches the shelf. It may sit there for weeks or months before a customer buys it. In between, rent, rates, wages and card fees still have to be paid. Any weak season, a warm winter for a coat shop for example, leaves the retailer holding paid-for stock that has not turned back into cash.

Because retailers are paid at the till, invoice finance rarely fits unless there is a trade or wholesale side. The usual options are a revolving credit facility to draw on when stock is bought and repay as it sells, a merchant cash advance repaid from card takings, and a short-term unsecured loan to get through a slow patch. Some lenders will also look at the stock itself as security, which is a specialist area.
uses: Buying ahead of the peak
Order autumn and Christmas stock in the summer, when supplier deposits are due and the shop is at its quietest.
Paying suppliers early for a discount
Settle with a supplier on shorter terms to win a better unit price, and recover the cost as the stock sells.
Covering a slow season
Keep rent, rates and wages paid through a weak few months, such as January after a heavy Christmas.
Clearance and returns
Absorb the cost of unsold stock and customer returns without cutting into the money set aside for the next order.
fit: A limit that moves with stock

A revolving credit facility of, for example, £25,000 to £100,000 lets a retailer draw when a stock order is paid for and repay as the goods sell. Interest applies only to what is drawn, which suits a business whose borrowing swings across the year.
Repayments from the till

A merchant cash advance is repaid as a share of card sales, so an empty week costs less than a full one. Lenders look at monthly card volume rather than profit, which can help shops with thin margins but steady footfall. The total repayable is higher than the amount advanced.
Stock as security

Stock finance, where the goods themselves secure the borrowing, exists but suits retailers with high-value, easy-to-resell items such as furniture, jewellery or electronics. Fashion and seasonal lines are harder to value, so lenders may advance a smaller share of cost.
considerations: Slow-moving stock is the real problem
If borrowing is covering stock that is not selling, adding more only delays a markdown decision. Lenders will look at stock turn, so know yours.
Peak-to-trough repayments
A fixed loan repayment is the same in January as in December. A flexible or card-linked product may suit a seasonal shop better than a fixed term.
Personal guarantees and charges
Retail facilities often carry a director’s guarantee. A broker will explain what applies, so you can decide with the risk in view.
faqs: Can a shop use invoice finance?

Only if it sells to other businesses on credit terms, as in a wholesale or trade side. Over-the-counter sales are paid immediately, so there are no invoices to finance. A broker can explain the options for a retailer that mixes the two, and suggest alternatives such as revolving credit.
How do lenders judge a retailer’s working capital request?

They look at bank statements, card takings, stock levels, supplier terms and the lease. They want to see steady sales through the year and how the shop copes with its quiet months. Accounts showing profit are helpful, but lenders also look closely at cash flow.
What is stock finance?

It is borrowing secured against inventory, so the goods themselves act as security. It suits retailers with valuable, resaleable stock. The lender sets a percentage of the stock’s cost or value, and monitors levels. It is a specialist product, so a broker with retail experience can say who offers it.
Is a merchant cash advance expensive for a shop?

It can cost more in total than a bank loan, because the repayable amount is a fixed sum above the advance. Repayments adjust to takings, which is its main benefit. A broker should show you the total cost and compare it with other options before you decide.
Do retailers on a high street lease find it harder to borrow?

A short lease can be a concern, since it limits the shop’s future. Lenders also consider the location, footfall and whether the lease is renewed. A broker can help present your trading history and lease position clearly to the right lenders.

business-expansion|retail.h1: Business expansion finance for retail businesses
business-expansion|retail.title: Business Expansion Finance for Retail Businesses | Loanleaf
business-expansion|retail.desc: How UK retailers finance a second shop, a refit or a move into new product lines, and which finance types suit. Get matched with a specialist broker, free.
business-expansion|retail.lead: A new shop needs a deposit, a fit-out and opening stock before it sells a single item.
intro: Opening a second shop is a bigger step than most retailers expect, because the costs arrive in a block: the lease deposit, shopfitting, signage, tills, a first order of stock and staff trained before the doors open. The cash drain lasts until the shop finds its customers, which can take a year. Lenders therefore look closely at how the existing shop is doing, since a strong store is the best argument that another can work.

Retail expansion rarely needs a single type of finance. Shopfitting and equipment are often financed through asset finance. A loan can cover the deposit and opening stock. A broader move, such as a new product range or a warehouse for online orders, may involve a term loan alongside a revolving facility for stock. The best structure is the one that leaves cash free for stock, which is what the shop actually sells.
uses: A second or third shop
Cover the lease deposit, fit-out, signage and opening stock for a new location.
A refit of the current shop
Update the layout, lighting and tills to lift average spend, and pay for the work over several years.
A new product range
Buy the first run of a new line, from a supplier that wants payment up front, before any of it sells.
A stockroom or warehouse
Take on space to hold more stock, handle online orders, or supply several shops from one place.
fit: Fit-out through asset finance or a term loan

Shopfittings are hard to repossess because they are fixed to a building, so lenders often prefer an unsecured term loan, for example £30,000 to £120,000 over three to five years. Tills, display equipment and vehicles are easier to finance as assets in their own right.
Opening stock through a facility

Opening stock is usually best financed by a revolving facility, since the amount needed changes as the shop settles in. A fixed loan would be sized on a guess. Lenders will look at stock turn at the first shop to judge how quickly the second will sell through.
Evidence for the lender

Expect to supply recent accounts, bank statements, a business plan with projected sales per square foot, and the lease terms for the new unit. A shop with a record of rising sales or margins at the first site is more convincing than a forecast on its own.
considerations: A second shop can dilute attention
A retailer who is on the shop floor at the first store has to hire for the second. Wages and management time should be in the budget, not an afterthought.
Lease commitments
A new lease may run for five or ten years with rent reviews. Lenders and brokers will consider whether the business could still meet repayments if the new site underperforms.
Online as an alternative
For some shops, growing online costs less than a second site. A broker may suggest comparing the two before committing to a lease.
faqs: Will a lender finance a retail shopfit?

Some will, but because a fit-out is fixed to the premises it cannot easily be repossessed, so lenders usually treat it as general borrowing. An unsecured term loan or secured loan is typical. Equipment such as tills and fridges can often be financed separately as assets.
How much can a retailer borrow to open a second shop?

It depends on the existing shop’s profits, the company’s age and the new site’s costs. As an illustration, a shop turning over £500,000 might look at £40,000 to £150,000. A broker can help work out what is sensible before you sign a lease.
Should I wait for the first shop to be profitable?

Most lenders will want to see that it is. They look at at least 12 months of accounts and bank statements to judge consistency. Trying to expand while the first shop is still breaking even raises the risk for both you and a lender.
Is stock finance different from a loan?

Yes. With stock finance, the goods are the security and the borrowing moves up and down with stock levels, as with a revolving facility. A loan is a fixed sum repaid over a set term. A broker can explain which suits your range and pace of selling.
Can I finance a move into e-commerce at the same time?

Yes, but each part is assessed on its own merits. Website development, a warehouse and extra stock may suit different finance. A broker used to retail can help structure the borrowing so the shops and the online side are each carried by the right product.

working-capital|manufacturing.title: Working Capital for Manufacturing Businesses | Loanleaf
working-capital|manufacturing.desc: How UK manufacturers cover raw materials, production time and customer payment terms, and and which finance types fit a factory cash cycle. Free introduction.
working-capital|manufacturing.lead: A manufacturer buys materials, pays wages through production, then waits for the customer to pay.
intro: Manufacturing has the longest cash cycle of most small businesses. Raw materials are bought, often on short supplier terms, then turned into finished goods over days or weeks, shipped, invoiced and finally paid for 30 to 60 days later. At every stage money is tied up, in raw stock, work in progress and finished goods, and the business still has to pay wages, energy and rent. A large order makes the squeeze worse, because the costs come first.

Since manufacturers usually sell to other businesses on invoice, invoice finance is often the first option to consider, as it releases cash against invoices already raised. A revolving credit facility can fund the buying of materials, and some lenders offer stock or purchase finance for raw materials. For sudden jumps in cost, such as a metal price spike, a short-term unsecured loan may help bridge the gap. A broker who knows manufacturing can explain which suits your production cycle and customers.
uses: Raw materials for a big order
Buy steel, plastic, timber or components for a large order, when the supplier wants paying before the customer pays you.
Long customer payment terms
Free up cash from invoices that large buyers pay in 60 or 90 days, so the factory is not waiting on them.
Bridging a price spike
Absorb a sudden rise in materials or energy costs while selling prices catch up.
Smoothing uneven orders
Keep staff and production lines running between bulk orders without laying anyone off.
fit: Invoice finance for B2B sales

A lender advances most of the value of approved invoices, often 80% to 90%, and pays the balance, less fees, when the customer settles. It scales with sales, so a larger order releases more cash. It suits manufacturers with a spread of reliable business customers, and lenders assess the customers’ credit as well as yours.
Financing the materials side

Buying materials in bulk can be supported through a revolving facility or purchase finance, where a lender pays the supplier and you repay when the goods are sold. Lenders look at how long raw materials sit before they turn into invoices, so know your production cycle.
Export orders

If you sell abroad, export invoice finance and trade finance can cover the longer shipping and payment times, and may include credit protection. A broker with manufacturing and export experience will know which providers handle overseas customers.
considerations: Concentration risk
If one customer makes up most of your sales, invoice finance can be harder to get or limited in size. Lenders may cap the amount against a single debtor.
Stock is harder to borrow against
Work in progress is difficult to value. Finished goods are easier but still need a ready market. Expect lenders to advance less against stock than against invoices.
Costs add up
Invoice finance has service fees and interest. A broker can show the full cost, which you can compare with the margin you earn on the order.
faqs: Is invoice finance suitable for a manufacturer?

Often, yes, because manufacturers raise invoices to other businesses, usually on 30 to 90-day terms. Lenders advance against those invoices and take their fees as customers pay. It works best with a spread of customers with good credit, and the lender will check them as well as your company.
Can I borrow against raw materials or work in progress?

Some lenders offer stock or purchase finance, but they usually advance less against materials and work in progress than against invoices, because these are harder to value and sell. Finished goods with a ready market are easier. A specialist broker can say who offers this.
What does a lender look at for a manufacturing business?

Accounts, bank statements, aged debtors and creditors, the order book, and the customer list. Lenders also consider how reliable your production is, and how exposed you are to a single customer or supplier. They want to see profit and cash flow, not only turnover.
How much working capital might a small factory need?

As a rough illustration, a manufacturer with £2m annual sales and 60-day customer terms could have £300,000 or more tied up in unpaid invoices at any time. Facility size is set by lenders based on the business’s own figures, so a broker is the best guide.
Will a lender take a charge over my machinery?

Some might, particularly if the borrowing is larger or secured. Others rely on a debenture over the whole company or a personal guarantee. If you have already financed machinery, existing lenders may have priority. A broker can explain how your current arrangements affect new borrowing.

business-expansion|manufacturing.title: Business Expansion Finance for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
business-expansion|manufacturing.desc: How UK manufacturers finance new production lines, larger premises and capacity for bigger orders, and which finance types suit. Free introduction to a broker.
business-expansion|manufacturing.lead: More capacity means new machines, bigger premises and extra staff well before the larger orders arrive.
intro: Expanding a manufacturing business is capital heavy. A new production line, a bigger unit or a second shift costs money long before the extra output is sold, and machines are often ordered months ahead of delivery. Once capacity is in place, the larger volumes also need more materials and wages, and customers still pay on terms. Many manufacturers find the equipment is the easy part to finance, and the working capital to run it is the real stretch.

Because machinery holds a value, asset finance is usually the natural route for the equipment, with the machine as security and a term of up to its useful life. Premises may be financed with a commercial mortgage. The extra working capital is often better handled with invoice finance or a revolving facility, which grow with sales. Splitting the plan into these parts tends to cost less than a single large loan.
uses: A new production line
Buy CNC machines, presses, packaging lines or ovens to raise output or make a new product.
Moving to a bigger unit
Take on a larger factory or add a mezzanine, loading bay or cold store as orders outgrow the space.
A big new contract
Staff and stock for a major customer whose volumes are larger than anything you have made before.
Automation and efficiency
Install robotics, new software or energy-saving plant to cut cost per unit and compete on price.
fit: Machinery through asset finance

Lenders often advance most of the price of new or used machinery, with repayments over three to seven years, and with the asset as security. Specialist machinery with a narrow resale market is harder to finance, so lenders look at who else would buy it. Used kit with a track record can be easier to value.
Premises through a commercial mortgage

Buying a unit might involve a deposit of 25% or more and a term of up to 25 years. Lenders look at the property’s use and value, and whether profits cover the repayment comfortably. Some owners buy the premises through a separate property company, which a broker can discuss.
Working capital for higher volumes

A first large order can strain cash even if it is profitable. Invoice finance scales with the extra invoices, and a revolving facility handles materials. Lenders may want to see contracts or purchase orders as evidence the extra capacity will be used.
considerations: Delivery and commissioning delays
Machines can arrive late or take weeks to commission. Repayments may start before the line is earning, so ask whether a payment holiday or staged drawdown is available.
Reliance on one customer
Expanding for a single big buyer ties your fortunes to theirs. Lenders will consider how the business would manage if that order fell away.
Grants and tax allowances
Capital allowances or grants may reduce the real cost of machinery. This is a question for an accountant, but it can change how much you need to borrow.
faqs: Can I finance second-hand machinery?

Yes, many asset finance lenders do. They look at the age, condition and make of the machine, and whether it has a ready resale market. Older or niche machinery may mean a larger deposit or shorter term. A broker can find lenders comfortable with the type of equipment you need.
How long is a typical term for machinery finance?

Terms of three to seven years are common, matched to the machine’s working life. Longer terms lower monthly cost but raise the total paid. Lenders do not want the loan to outlast the useful life of the asset, so shorter lives mean shorter terms.
Do I need a deposit for a production line?

Often a deposit of 10% to 20% is asked for, though it varies by lender, the asset and the strength of the business. Some lenders advance the full cost against strong accounts. A broker can say what is realistic for the equipment you have in mind.
Should the factory be bought or rented?

Buying gives a long-term asset and fixes the cost, but needs a deposit and ties up capital. Renting keeps cash free for machines and stock. Lenders on a commercial mortgage will look at your profits and the property. It is worth discussing with an accountant and a broker.
What if a large order is cancelled after I have bought the machine?

The repayments continue, because the loan is with the lender, not the customer. This is why many brokers advise matching expansion to confirmed orders or a spread of customers. If you are concerned, ask about shorter terms or leasing, which may give more flexibility.

working-capital|transport-and-logistics.h1: Working capital finance for transport and logistics
working-capital|transport-and-logistics.title: Working Capital for Transport and Logistics | Loanleaf
working-capital|transport-and-logistics.desc: How UK hauliers and logistics firms cover fuel, wages and driver costs while customers pay on 30 to 90 days, and which finance suits. Free introduction.
working-capital|transport-and-logistics.lead: Fuel, wages and tolls are paid weekly, but the customer’s invoice is paid weeks or months later.
intro: A haulier pays for diesel at the pump, drivers every week and tyres, tolls and maintenance as they arise. The customer, often a large retailer or manufacturer, pays 30, 60 or even 90 days after the delivery. With fuel one of the biggest costs, a firm running ten trucks can have tens of thousands of pounds out on the road before the first invoice is settled. Margins are thin, so a single late payer can leave a profitable firm short.

This pattern is why invoice finance is so common in transport. Lenders advance cash against delivered, proof-of-delivery invoices, which are easy to verify. Some firms add a fuel card facility or a revolving credit facility to smooth the week-to-week costs. For a sudden bill, such as an MOT failure or a tax payment, a short-term unsecured loan can help. A broker used to the sector will know which providers understand haulage.
uses: Fuel and driver wages every week
Pay for diesel and drivers on a weekly cycle while invoices to customers run to 60 or 90 days.
A slow-paying major customer
Release cash from invoices owed by a large retailer or manufacturer that settles at the end of its terms.
Unplanned repairs and tyres
Cover a gearbox, a set of tyres or an MOT failure without taking a truck off the road for lack of cash.
Seasonal peaks
Pay for extra agency drivers, fuel and subcontractors in the run-up to Christmas, when work is heavy and payment still lags.
fit: Invoice finance on proof of delivery

Lenders often advance up to 85% to 90% of the value of invoices backed by signed delivery notes, and release the rest, less fees, when the customer pays. Because haulage invoices are frequent and well documented, they tend to suit invoice finance. Selective facilities let you finance only certain customers’ invoices.
Fuel and weekly costs

Some firms add a fuel card with extended credit terms, or a revolving credit facility sized to a few weeks of running costs. A facility of, for example, £50,000 to £200,000 can ride out the gap between a delivery and a payment. Lenders assess the number of vehicles, revenue and the quality of customers.
One-off shortfalls

A short unsecured loan can cover a particular bill, such as a tax payment or major repair. Terms are often a few months to two years. Lenders will look at bank statements and look closely at how stable the weekly cash pattern is.
considerations: Customer concentration
If one retailer accounts for most revenue, a lender may limit how much they will advance against it. Spreading the customer base helps.
Fuel price swings
A sharp rise in diesel prices can squeeze cash quickly. Check whether your contracts include fuel surcharges before relying on borrowing to bridge it.
Fees on small invoices
Invoice finance fees can feel heavy if margins are narrow. Ask a broker for the all-in cost per invoice before committing.
faqs: Is invoice finance common in haulage?

Yes, it is widely used. Haulage invoices are backed by proof of delivery, and customers are often large, creditworthy firms, which lenders like. Some providers specialise in the sector and offer features such as fuel credit. A broker can show you who has experience with transport businesses.
Can I finance only some of my customers’ invoices?

Often yes, through selective or spot invoice finance. You choose which invoices to finance, for example the slow-paying ones, and pay fees only on those. Whole-ledger arrangements finance every invoice and may suit firms with a steady need. A broker can explain the difference and the costs involved.
How do lenders view owner-drivers and small fleets?

They look at the contracts you have, how many vehicles you operate, and your payment history. A small fleet with solid contracts is often fine, but reliance on one customer or spot work can limit what lenders will offer. Accounts and bank statements are used to judge consistency of income.
What if a customer goes bust owing me money?

With non-recourse invoice finance or credit protection, the lender may absorb part of the loss. With recourse arrangements, you usually repay the advance. This is an important difference, so ask a broker which type you are being offered and what it costs.
How much working capital does a small haulier need?

It varies. As an illustration, a firm running five trucks with £40,000 a month in costs and customers paying in 60 days might need £80,000 or more to bridge the gap. Lenders will assess this from your own accounts, so a broker can help size a facility.

business-expansion|transport-and-logisti.h1: Business expansion finance for transport and logistics
business-expansion|transport-and-logisti.title: Business Expansion Finance for Transport and Logistics | Loanleaf
business-expansion|transport-and-logisti.desc: How UK haulage and logistics firms finance extra trucks, trailers and a bigger depot, and which finance types tend to suit. Free introduction to a broker.
business-expansion|transport-and-logisti.lead: Every extra truck needs a driver, insurance and fuel before the contract that justifies it starts paying.
intro: A haulier that wins a bigger contract has to add vehicles and drivers before the first load. A new tractor unit can cost well over £80,000, a trailer another £25,000 or more, and each needs a driver, insurance, tax and tracking from day one. Contracts often start with a trial period, and payment terms of 30 to 60 days mean it can be a quarter before cash comes back. Depot space, an operator’s licence and a bigger transport office can add to the cost.

Vehicles are the easiest part of the plan to finance, since each truck or trailer is a hard asset that lenders can value and recover. Hire purchase and leasing are the standard routes. A yard or warehouse may suit a commercial mortgage. The extra working capital to carry bigger payrolls and fuel bills usually comes from invoice finance or a revolving facility. A broker who understands the sector can match each need to the right product.
uses: Adding tractor units and trailers
Buy or lease extra vehicles to take on a new contract or a larger share of an existing one.
A new depot or yard
Take on a site closer to customers, or buy the yard you currently rent to protect against rent rises.
Moving into temperature-controlled or specialist haulage
Invest in refrigerated trailers, ADR vehicles or tail-lift units to serve higher-value customers.
A warehouse and fulfilment offer
Add storage and pick-and-pack space to move from pure haulage into a wider logistics service.
fit: Vehicles through hire purchase or leasing

HP usually covers most of a truck’s price with a deposit, over three to five years, and the vehicle is the security. Leasing keeps repayments lower and may suit firms that renew fleets often. Lenders look at the make and age of the vehicle, and at your operator’s licence and trading history.
Yard or depot through a commercial mortgage

A site may be financed with a deposit of 25% or more and a term of 10 to 25 years. Yards can raise planning and environmental questions that lenders check closely. Some firms prefer to keep renting while the contract base grows, so it is worth testing both routes.
Working capital for a growing fleet

Extra trucks mean more weekly costs on top of the finance repayments. Invoice finance can release cash from the first invoices of the new contract, and a revolving facility can smooth fuel and wages. Lenders will often ask to see the new contract before agreeing any limits.
considerations: Contract risk
A truck is repaid whether or not the contract continues. If a customer ends or cuts a contract, the vehicle payments remain. Where possible, expand against longer or multi-customer contracts.
Driver shortages
Vehicles without drivers earn nothing. Build recruitment and agency cover into the cost of expansion.
Residual values
Used truck values can move with the market. For leases, ask how end-of-term values are set and what happens if the vehicle is worth less than expected.
faqs: Should a haulier use hire purchase or leasing?

HP leads to ownership once the payments are made, which suits trucks you intend to keep. Leasing usually has lower monthly payments and you return the vehicle, which may suit a regularly renewed fleet. Tax and VAT treatment differ, so a broker and an accountant can help you choose.
Do lenders want a contract before financing a new truck?

Many do, or at least evidence of demand. For a first extra vehicle, a good trading record may be enough. For larger additions, lenders look for contracts, purchase orders or letters of intent to be sure the truck will be used. A broker can explain what is needed.
Can I finance a trailer separately from the tractor unit?

Yes. Each is a separate asset and can be financed on its own terms. Trailers often have longer working lives and hold value, so terms may be longer. This lets you add capacity in stages, rather than financing a full vehicle set in one go.
What does an operator’s licence have to do with finance?

Lenders will want to know you hold the right licence for the number of vehicles you operate, and that your compliance record is clean. Increasing fleet size may require a variation of the licence. A broker can explain what a lender will check as part of the application.
How big a depot do I need before buying makes sense?

There is no fixed rule. Buying makes more sense when you are confident of staying at the location for many years and have the deposit. Many growing firms rent first. A commercial mortgage broker can compare the running cost of owning and renting for your site.

working-capital|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Working capital finance for healthcare and dental practices
working-capital|healthcare-and-dental.title: Working Capital for Healthcare and Dental | Loanleaf
working-capital|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How UK dental, GP, physio and care practices cover wages, lab fees and NHS payment timing, and which finance types may suit. Free introduction to a broker.
working-capital|healthcare-and-dental.lead: Staff, lab fees and equipment leases are paid monthly, while NHS and insurer payments arrive on their own schedule.
intro: A dental or healthcare practice has high fixed costs: clinical staff, nurses, rent, indemnity and equipment leases. Income can arrive through several routes, patient fees at the chair, private insurers who pay after a delay, and NHS contracts paid monthly in arrears or adjusted at year end. If a contract payment is late, or insurers are slow, the practice still has to run payroll. Practices that are growing a patient list also carry the cost of new clinicians before the patients arrive.

Practices tend to borrow in a way that follows how they are paid. Invoice finance can suit those with large insurer or care-home invoices. A revolving credit facility gives a buffer for payroll and lab bills, and a short-term unsecured loan can cover a one-off cost such as a clinician’s signing bonus or the gap before a new contract starts. Because practices are generally stable and profitable, many lenders view them favourably.
uses: Payroll while an insurer or contract pays late
Cover clinical and admin wages while private insurers or a commissioning body settle invoices.
Lab and materials bills
Pay dental labs, suppliers and consumables on terms while patient fees arrive later or are paid in instalments.
Onboarding a new clinician
Pay a new dentist, hygienist or physio for several months while their patient list builds up.
A gap between contract years
Keep the practice afloat while an NHS contract is renewed or adjusted at year end.
fit: A facility sized to monthly payroll

A revolving credit facility covering one to two months of staff and fixed costs, for example £40,000 to £150,000, gives a safety net without borrowing a fixed sum. Lenders look closely at the practice’s revenue mix, how reliably payments arrive, and how much comes from NHS contracts versus private care.
Invoice finance for larger payers

If a care or occupational health provider bills insurers, employers or local authorities, invoice finance can release cash against those invoices. It is less relevant to practices paid mainly at the point of care by patients, where there is no invoice to finance.
Short loans for known costs

A short unsecured loan, perhaps £10,000 to £50,000 over one to three years, can cover a specific cost. Lenders often look favourably on healthcare practices because income is dependable and demand is steady, though they will check the practice’s accounts and director’s history.
considerations: Contract dependence
A practice that depends heavily on one NHS contract carries risk if it is reduced or not renewed. Lenders will ask about contract terms and renewal dates.
Patient list takes time
New clinicians take months to fill their diaries. Borrow for a realistic ramp-up, not a best-case one.
Regulatory costs
CQC registration, indemnity and compliance have to be met whatever the cash position. A broker may suggest including them in any borrowing plan.
faqs: Do lenders like dental and healthcare businesses?

Many do, because income is steady and demand does not fall away in downturns the way discretionary spending does. They still check accounts, contracts and the owners’ track record. A practice with a good patient base and clean records is usually seen more favourably than average, though terms vary lender by lender.
How does NHS contract income affect borrowing?

Lenders see it as reliable but fixed. They will ask about the contract’s value, length and clawback terms. Payments in arrears and year-end adjustments can create gaps, which working capital borrowing is designed to bridge. A broker can present the contract position clearly to lenders.
Can a practice use invoice finance?

If it raises invoices to insurers, employers or other organisations, yes. If most income comes from patients paying at the time, there are no invoices to finance. A broker can say whether your income mix makes it worthwhile, or whether a revolving facility is a better fit.
Is a personal guarantee required?

Often for smaller practices, yes, particularly for unsecured lending. Lenders may ask the principal dentist or directors to guarantee the borrowing. A broker should explain what any guarantee commits you to before you sign, and whether other structures are available for the amount you are borrowing.
How much working capital might a dental practice need?

It depends on size. As an illustration, a practice with £1m turnover and £70,000 monthly costs might want a buffer of one to two months of costs. Lenders will set the actual limit using the practice’s figures, so a broker can provide a better sense after hearing the details.

business-expansion|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Business expansion finance for healthcare and dental practices
business-expansion|healthcare-and-dental.title: Business Expansion Finance for Healthcare and Dental | Loanleaf
business-expansion|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How UK dental and healthcare practices finance new surgeries, equipment, a second site or an acquisition, and which finance suits. Free introduction.
business-expansion|healthcare-and-dental.lead: A new surgery needs equipment, fit-out and a clinician before the first patient in the chair.
intro: Expanding a practice usually means adding clinical capacity: another surgery, a second site, a new treatment room or an acquired practice. A dental surgery fitted out with chair, X-ray, compressor, instruments and decontamination space can cost well over £100,000, and a new clinician’s list takes months to fill. There are also compliance costs, such as CQC registration, radiation protection and sterilisation standards, which must be met before a patient is treated.

Healthcare equipment holds value and is easy to value, so asset finance is the common route for chairs, scanners and other kit. A fit-out or an acquisition may suit a term loan or a commercial mortgage, particularly where the practice owns the freehold. Acquisitions are a specialist area, and lenders usually lend against the goodwill and trading record of the target practice, so a broker who knows the sector is valuable.
uses: A new surgery or treatment room
Fit out an extra room with chair, delivery unit, imaging and storage to raise capacity in your existing site.
Digital dentistry and imaging
Buy intra-oral scanners, CBCT or 3D printers that bring work in-house and raise the range of treatments offered.
Buying another practice
Acquire a retiring principal’s practice, including goodwill, patient list and equipment.
A second site or clinic
Open a new location, with fit-out, equipment and the first months of staff costs before it earns.
fit: Equipment through asset finance

Dental chairs, scanners and imaging kit are often financed over five to seven years, with the equipment as security. Some lenders offer healthcare-specific terms. They will look at the make and supplier, and at the practice’s accounts, since stable healthcare income is generally viewed well.
Acquisitions and goodwill

A practice purchase often involves a large share of the price as goodwill, which is not a physical asset. Specialist lenders will lend against the target’s trading record, patient numbers and NHS or private mix. Terms of 10 to 15 years are common, often with a deposit from the buyer.
Fit-out and property

If the practice owns or is buying its premises, a commercial mortgage may be suitable. Leasehold fit-out is usually financed by a term loan. Lenders will want accounts, a business plan with projected patient numbers, and, for NHS work, details of contract capacity.
considerations: Clinician availability
A new surgery needs a clinician to staff it. Recruitment can be slow and costly, so build in time and salary before income begins.
NHS capacity is not guaranteed
Adding a room does not mean more NHS activity. Contract levels are set separately, so check what extra income you can realistically earn.
Acquisition due diligence
Buying a practice means checking its patient numbers, records and compliance. Professional advice from an accountant and solicitor is worthwhile.
faqs: Can I borrow to buy another dental practice?

Yes, specialist lenders do this regularly. They lend against the practice’s trading record and goodwill, and will want a deposit from the buyer, normally with the purchase price supported by a professional valuation. A broker who works with dental purchases can explain the process and the lenders involved.
Is goodwill difficult to finance?

It is less tangible than equipment or property, so lenders look carefully at the practice’s history, patient base and profits. Healthcare lenders understand the sector and are comfortable with goodwill if the figures are strong. Expect a deposit and a clear case for how the practice will keep its patients.
What equipment can be financed for a clinic?

Chairs, scanners, X-ray units, compressors, lasers, and physio or diagnostic equipment can all typically be financed. New and used kit is possible, and software is sometimes included. A broker can help compare terms and check whether the supplier works with particular finance providers.
Does opening a second site need a new CQC registration?

Usually, yes, a new location needs its own registration and checks before patients can be treated. This takes time and should be built into your timeline and budget. A broker or adviser can explain how a lender will treat the period before the new site earns.
How do lenders judge a plan for a new surgery?

They look at how full the existing diaries are, the patient waiting list, local demand and the cost of the new room. If current surgeries are consistently full, the case is stronger. A lender will also check profits, to see that repayments can be met comfortably.

working-capital|ecommerce.h1: Working capital finance for ecommerce businesses
working-capital|ecommerce.title: Working Capital for Ecommerce Businesses | Loanleaf
working-capital|ecommerce.desc: How UK online sellers finance stock, ad spend and marketplace payout delays, and which finance types suit an ecommerce cash cycle. Free introduction.
working-capital|ecommerce.lead: Stock and advertising are paid for up front, while marketplace payouts and returns arrive later.
intro: An online retailer pays a manufacturer, often overseas, weeks before stock is on the warehouse shelf, then spends on advertising to sell it. Customers pay at checkout, but the money may be held by a payment processor or marketplace for days, and returns are refunded from cash that has already gone. The cash cycle from paying a supplier to banking sales can run to three or four months, and a fast-growing store needs more cash tied up in stock the faster it grows.

The useful finance tends to be flexible. A revolving credit facility can be drawn when a stock order is placed and repaid as sales come in. A merchant cash advance can be repaid as a share of card and payment processor sales. Where the business sells wholesale or to retailers on credit, invoice finance may fit that side. For a particular order or peak, a short unsecured loan is common. A broker used to ecommerce can look at the data lenders see, such as processor payouts.
uses: Placing a large stock order
Pay a supplier or manufacturer in advance for a production run that will take months to arrive and sell.
Ahead of Black Friday and Christmas
Buy stock and ad budget in the autumn, when cash is tight and the biggest sales are still weeks away.
Marketplace payout delays
Cover costs while Amazon, eBay or a payment processor holds funds before releasing them to your account.
Advertising that pays back slowly
Keep paid social and search running at a level that wins customers, while the return on each customer arrives over months.
fit: A facility that follows stock cycles

A revolving credit facility of, for example, £30,000 to £150,000 can be drawn when a stock order is paid and repaid as sales clear. Lenders look at monthly revenue, gross margin, return rates and how consistently the business trades. Some use data from your accounting software and payment processors.
Repayment from payment processor sales

A merchant cash advance suits businesses with steady card or processor volume, and is repaid as a percentage of those sales. Repayments fall in slow weeks, though the total repayable is higher than the amount advanced. A broker can show you the full cost against other options.
Inventory and purchase finance

Some lenders pay suppliers directly and you repay as the stock sells. This can suit sellers who import goods and need to pay overseas manufacturers before shipping. Lenders look at the supplier relationship, the product and how fast it has sold previously.
considerations: Ad spend is not an asset
Lenders prefer lending against stock or invoices, which they can see. Borrowing to pay for advertising rests on your returns, so be ready to show margins and customer value.
Platform dependence
If most sales go through one marketplace, a change to its terms or an account suspension can hit cash quickly. Lenders may ask about this risk.
Returns and chargebacks
A high return rate eats into cash. Lenders and brokers will look at net sales, so know your return figures.
faqs: Can an online seller borrow against Amazon or Shopify sales?

Yes, some lenders use data from marketplaces and payment processors to assess a business and offer facilities or advances based on sales. Others use bank statements and accounts in the usual way. A broker can explain which lenders are comfortable with your sales channels.
How do lenders view a business that has only traded for a year?

The company must have been trading for at least six months. Lenders will look at the record you have, which should show growing, consistent sales and sensible margins. Fast growth can raise questions about stock and cash needs, so be ready to explain how the business is run and how stock turns.
What is the difference between a revolving facility and a loan for stock?

A loan is a fixed sum repaid over a set term. A revolving facility gives a limit that you draw on and repay as needed, paying interest on what you use. For stock that is ordered and sold in cycles, a revolving facility often follows the business more closely.
Can I get finance for paid advertising?

Some lenders will provide general working capital that you can use for advertising, though they usually assess the business’s overall performance rather than the campaign. Because ad spend gives no asset to secure, terms may be shorter or costlier. A broker can show your options.
Do I need a personal guarantee?

Often, particularly for unsecured or smaller facilities. Some lenders accept a debenture over company assets instead. A broker will explain what each lender requires and what a guarantee would mean for you personally, before you decide whether to go ahead with an offer.

business-expansion|ecommerce.h1: Business expansion finance for ecommerce businesses
business-expansion|ecommerce.title: Business Expansion Finance for Ecommerce Businesses | Loanleaf
business-expansion|ecommerce.desc: How UK online businesses finance a warehouse, new product ranges, new markets or an acquisition, and which finance types suit. Free introduction to a broker.
business-expansion|ecommerce.lead: Moving from a spare room to a warehouse, or into new markets, costs money well before the sales arrive.
intro: Ecommerce growth tends to arrive in steps. A seller outgrows a spare room and takes a small warehouse, then adds a pick-and-pack team, then a new product range or a second country. Each step needs cash for deposits, racking, staff and stock, and sales in the new market or range take months to build. Expansion into Europe, for instance, can involve a new VAT registration, a fulfilment partner, translation and local returns handling before the first order ships.

Online businesses have fewer hard assets than most, so lenders place weight on trading history, margins and customer data. Unsecured term loans are common, and asset finance covers racking, packing machinery and vehicles. Buying a smaller competitor or a brand is another route, which may involve a larger loan. Stock for the new range often needs a revolving facility, so the working capital can flex with the sales that follow.
uses: A warehouse and fulfilment team
Take on a unit with racking, packing stations and staff, or fund a move to a larger one as order volumes rise.
A new product range
Pay for design, samples, the first production run and a launch campaign before the range has sold anything.
Selling in a new country
Cover translation, local VAT set-up, fulfilment and returns for a European or US launch.
Buying a smaller brand
Acquire a competitor’s store, customer list and stock to add revenue and customers faster than building from scratch.
fit: An unsecured term loan on trading history

Lenders often offer £25,000 to £250,000 over one to five years to online businesses with solid accounts, based on revenue, margin and growth. Without property or large assets, they rely on the company’s figures and a director’s guarantee. A strong repeat-customer rate helps the case.
Racking and equipment through asset finance

Racking, conveyor systems, label printers, forklifts and vans can be financed with the equipment as security. This keeps the unsecured borrowing for stock and marketing. Used equipment is often easier to finance than people expect, since lenders understand its resale value.
Acquisitions

Buying another online business involves valuing its profits, stock and customer base. Lenders will often lend against the target’s trading record as well as yours, sometimes with the seller leaving part of the price to be paid later. Acquisitions are specialist, so a broker with experience can help.
considerations: Growth that outpaces stock cash
More sales means more stock paid for in advance. Plan the working capital for the larger sales volume as well as the capital spend.
New markets carry hidden costs
Returns, VAT, customs and carrier costs can be higher abroad. Include them in the case you show a lender.
Concentration on one channel
If most sales come from one platform or one ad channel, lenders may see the business as more fragile. Diversifying helps.
faqs: Will lenders finance an online business with no property?

Yes. They look at trading history, margins, repeat customers and the owners rather than assets. Unsecured lending is common, sometimes with a director’s guarantee. Equipment such as racking or vehicles can be financed separately as assets. A broker can explain which lenders understand ecommerce.
How much do lenders expect to see in sales history?

At least six months of trading is needed, and many prefer 12 months or more to see a full seasonal cycle, including peak periods. Monthly sales data, margins and return rates are useful. A broker can help you prepare the figures in the way lenders expect.
Can I borrow to buy another online business?

Yes, though it is a more specialist request. Lenders examine the target’s profits, stock and customer base, and may want valuation support. Terms might include a deposit from you and sometimes a deferred payment to the seller. A broker with acquisition experience can help.
Should I finance a warehouse move through a loan or asset finance?

Probably both. The racking, packing machinery and vehicles can be financed as assets, while a loan or facility covers the deposit, moving costs and extra staff. Splitting them often costs less and keeps the repayments aligned with the life of each item.
What if the new market does not sell as well as planned?

Repayments continue regardless. This is why many brokers suggest testing a new market before borrowing heavily, and keeping the term long enough that repayments stay manageable if sales are slow. Lenders may ask how the business would cope if the launch took longer than forecast.

working-capital|professional-services.h1: Working capital finance for professional services firms
working-capital|professional-services.title: Working Capital for Professional Services | Loanleaf
working-capital|professional-services.desc: How UK agencies, consultancies, recruiters and accountants cover payroll while clients pay on 30 to 90 days, and which finance types suit. Free introduction.
working-capital|professional-services.lead: Salaries are paid at month end, while client invoices may not be paid for another one to three months.
intro: A professional services firm has few materials to buy. Its main cost is people, paid monthly and on time, while the work is billed after delivery and often paid 30 to 90 days later. A firm of 20 staff on a £1m payroll can have hundreds of thousands tied up in unpaid fees. Billing may also depend on timesheets, milestones or retained work, and larger clients, such as corporates and the public sector, are known for slow payment runs.

Since the money owed is mostly on invoices, invoice finance is a common fit, and it can scale with billings. Recruitment firms often use it, since they pay contractors weekly and bill clients monthly. Where invoices are less regular, a revolving credit facility or a short unsecured loan can smooth the gap. Because professional firms hold few physical assets, lenders rely on trading history, client quality and bank statements to decide.
uses: Payroll while clients pay late
Pay salaries or contractors on time while invoices sit with large clients on 60 or 90-day terms.
A contractor payroll for recruiters
Pay temps and contractors weekly while your client pays monthly and sometimes later.
Winning a large retainer
Add staff and tools to deliver a big new client before their first payment arrives.
A quarterly tax bill
Cover VAT, corporation tax or PAYE when it falls due before the invoices that fund it are paid.
fit: Invoice finance for fee billing

Lenders advance a large share of approved invoices, often 80% to 90%, and release the rest less fees when the client pays. Invoices for completed work with clear terms are easiest to finance. Work billed in advance, or subject to milestones not yet met, may not qualify.
Payroll-led facilities for recruiters

Recruitment firms often use invoice finance designed around contractor payroll, with funds available the same week the timesheet is approved. These products can include payroll and credit control services, and are priced accordingly. A broker who knows recruitment can compare them.
A revolving facility or short loan

For firms with fewer, larger clients, a revolving credit facility of, for example, £25,000 to £100,000 may give flexibility without financing every invoice. Lenders will look at the length of the client relationships, the mix of retained and project work, and profit margin.
considerations: Client concentration
If one client pays most of your fees, a lender may limit how much they advance against that client. The lender will also want to know the client is creditworthy.
Disclosure to clients
Some invoice finance is disclosed, so clients pay the lender. Others are confidential. For a relationship-led firm, this can matter, so ask a broker which options are discreet.
Margins and cost
Fees on invoice finance are a percentage of turnover. For high-margin consultancies this is easy to absorb, but for thin-margin recruitment it needs careful costing.
faqs: Is invoice finance common for agencies and consultancies?

Yes. Fee invoices are usually for completed work and owed by other businesses, which suits invoice finance. Lenders look at the client list, payment history and the nature of the work. Some firms prefer a revolving facility, which does not involve the clients. A broker can compare the two for you.
Do clients need to know I am using invoice finance?

Not always. Confidential arrangements let you collect payment as normal, while disclosed ones ask the client to pay the lender. Confidential facilities usually suit firms with a stronger track record and may cost more. A broker can say which providers offer discretion.
How do recruiters finance contractor payroll?

Many use invoice finance, with the lender advancing funds against approved timesheets or invoices so contractors are paid weekly. Some providers offer payroll and credit control as part of the service. Lenders assess the quality of your clients and the contractor model, including how timesheets are signed off.
What can I borrow against if I have no assets?

Professional firms rely on invoices, contracts and trading history rather than property or equipment. Unsecured loans and revolving facilities are common, often with a director’s guarantee. A strong record of profitable trading, repeat clients and prompt invoicing helps your case with lenders.
Can I borrow to pay a tax bill?

Yes, VAT and tax loans exist for this purpose, and a revolving facility or short loan can also be used. Lenders usually want to know you are able to repay, and may ask about the reason for the shortfall. A broker can explain the cost against the penalty for paying late.

business-expansion|professional-services.h1: Business expansion finance for professional services firms
business-expansion|professional-services.title: Business Expansion Finance for Professional Services | Loanleaf
business-expansion|professional-services.desc: How UK agencies, consultancies and practices finance new hires, offices, acquisitions and new service lines, and which finance suits. Free introduction.
business-expansion|professional-services.lead: Growing a firm of people means hiring months before the new clients pay for them.
intro: For a professional services firm, expansion is mostly a people decision. A new fee-earner or consultant can take three to six months to reach full billing, and a firm that adds five at once will carry several hundred thousand pounds of salary before the revenue appears. Other costs include an additional office, recruitment fees, software, training and professional indemnity insurance. An acquisition of another practice or client book can also be a fast route, though the price is usually a multiple of recurring fees.

With few hard assets, lenders look at the quality and consistency of fee income. Unsecured term loans, sometimes with a director’s guarantee, are common. Office fit-out and technology may suit asset finance. Buying a firm or client book is a specialist area, where lenders judge the retention of the fees being acquired. A revolving facility or invoice finance can then carry the extra payroll during the ramp-up, so that the expansion does not drain day-to-day cash.
uses: Hiring a team ahead of revenue
Pay a group of new fee-earners while they build up billable work and client relationships.
A second office
Open an office in another city to reach new clients, covering fit-out, rent and early salaries.
Buying a client book or practice
Acquire another firm, a retiring partner’s clients or a rival’s fee base, and pay in instalments from future income.
A new service line
Add a new discipline, such as cyber security for an IT firm or tax for an accountant, with the people and tools to deliver it.
fit: An unsecured loan against fee income

Lenders offer unsecured term loans, for example £50,000 to £300,000 over three to five years, based on turnover, profit and the stability of client revenue. Recurring retainers carry more weight than one-off projects. A director’s guarantee is common, and some lenders also take a debenture over the company.
Acquiring a firm or client book

Lenders look at how much of the acquired fee income is likely to stay after the sale. Retention rates, contract terms and the seller’s handover period all matter. Deals may include a deferred or earn-out element, so you pay part of the price from future fees, which can reduce the borrowing needed.
Fit-out and technology

Office equipment, IT hardware and software can often be financed through asset finance, with terms of two to five years. Some software and subscription costs can be hard to finance. Lenders typically treat them as general borrowing, so a broker can say where each item sits.
considerations: People are the asset, and they can leave
If key staff move, clients may follow. Lenders will look at how dependent the firm is on individuals, and may ask for key-person cover.
Slow ramp-up
New hires rarely reach target billing in the first quarter. Plan the borrowing to carry salaries for six months, not three.
Acquisition integration
Merging two firms takes management time and can lose clients. Budget for it, and take professional advice before buying.
faqs: Can a professional firm borrow without property or equipment?

Yes. Lenders can assess a firm on its fee income, margins, client retention and trading history. Unsecured loans are common, usually with a director’s guarantee. A firm with recurring retainers and low client concentration will usually look stronger than one that relies on project work.
How do lenders view a plan to hire a new team?

They look at how quickly new hires are expected to bill, the firm’s existing capacity to carry their salaries and the evidence of demand. A pipeline of signed work helps. Realistic assumptions are better received than optimistic ones, so build in a slower ramp-up than you hope for.
Can I finance the purchase of a client book?

Yes, specialist lenders do this, particularly for accountancy, financial services and similar firms. They look at the fees being acquired, how long clients have stayed and any handover arrangements. Part of the price is often deferred and paid from the fees the book generates.
Is asset finance useful for a services firm?

For computers, office fit-out, phones and some software, yes. It keeps the cost of equipment separate and spreads it over its useful life. The amounts are usually small compared with payroll, so most expansion borrowing for a services firm is general rather than asset-based.
What if a key partner or fee-earner leaves after expansion?

It can reduce fee income while the borrowing continues, so lenders look at key-person risk. Some ask for life or critical illness cover on principals. If your firm relies on one or two individuals, a broker can advise what lenders are likely to want in place.
